title: Kissing the leper
hook: Francis writes that what was bitter became sweet

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Benedictine day at home: bell, psalm, work, reading, meal and silence, kept in balance. Your line was balance.

Francis of Assisi left a short text now called his Testament, looking back at how it all began. A reader might expect a vision, a voice from heaven, a dramatic call. Instead he starts with his stomach. When he was living in sin, he says, the very sight of lepers was too bitter for him to bear. That's where the story of the Franciscans opens: not with a great deed, but with a man who couldn't stand to look at certain people. Benedict's cloister is behind us now; this is the road, and the friars. Today: kissing the leper.
screen: `FRANCIS LOOKS BACK.` → `NOT A VISION. A REVULSION.` → `OUT OF THE CLOISTER, ONTO THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's what Francis says happened. The Lord himself led him among the lepers, and he showed them mercy. And when he left them, what had seemed bitter to him was turned into sweetness, of soul and of body. Then, he says, he waited a little while, and left the world. A few lines, and in his own telling, the hinge of his whole life. Notice what he doesn't say. There's no kiss. The kiss comes from the stories his early biographers told. In their telling, Francis is riding near Assisi when he meets a leper on the road. Everything in him wants to turn the horse around. Instead he gets down, gives the man money, and kisses his hand, and the leper kisses him back. In some versions he then goes to the place where lepers lived and serves them there. Francis's own spare account, and the vivid scene the biographers drew: both land on the same turn. Look at who does what in the Testament. Francis doesn't say he conquered his disgust. He says the Lord led him. The change in his feelings came after the mercy, not before it. He didn't wait to feel sweetness before he went; the bitterness changed on the way out. That suggests the feeling of revulsion isn't a verdict. It can be the doorway. In the gospels Jesus touches a leper before he heals him.
screen: `THE LORD LED ME AMONG THEM.` · `WHAT WAS BITTER WAS TURNED TO SWEETNESS.` · `THE KISS COMES FROM THE BIOGRAPHERS.` · then, large: `BITTER BECAME SWEET.` · then: `THE FEELING CAME AFTER THE MERCY.`

segments.voice: Let one thing come to mind that makes you pull back, not something dangerous, just a call you've avoided or a person you steer around, and notice where the feeling sits in your body without arguing with it. Then picture yourself doing it anyway, gently, the way Francis got down from his horse, and see whether the picture changes the feeling at all. If you pray, ask to be led, the way Francis says he was.
Kissing the leper. The turning point Francis described in his Testament: what had seemed bitter to him was turned into sweetness, once he showed mercy. Today's word.
Your line: bitter became sweet. It began with being led, not with feeling brave. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: Franciscans tell the story of the leper as the start of Francis's conversion, and Franciscan friars and sisters still serve the sick and the poor in hospitals, shelters and missions.

chat.says: Did Francis love lepers right away, or did he have to get over his disgust first?
options: Neither. The sight was bitter to him, but the Lord led him to show mercy, and then it turned sweet.
He loved them with tenderness from childhood, which is why he was drawn to serve them so early.
He trained himself to feel no disgust at all first, and only then dared to go near them.
chat.meaning: In his Testament Francis says the Lord led him among lepers; after he showed mercy, what was bitter turned to sweetness. The feeling followed the mercy.

Testament.meaning: a short text Francis left, looking back on his life

lepers.meaning: people with leprosy, a disease once feared and shunned

friars.meaning: brothers in a religious order like Francis's

notes: The Testament is paraphrased: 'when I was in sins, it seemed too bitter to me to see lepers; the Lord himself led me among them and I showed mercy to them; and when I left them, what had seemed bitter to me was changed into sweetness of soul and body; afterward I waited a little and left the world.' Confirm the paraphrase.

The leper meeting with the kiss: Celano's Second Life 9 and Bonaventure's Major Legend 1.5 (and Celano's First Life 17 on serving lepers). Confirm references and details (dismounting, money, kiss of the hand, leper's kiss in return).
'Francis's first followers would come to spend time serving lepers' — confirm (Earlier Rule ch. 9 speaks of friars living among lepers).
Latin of the Testament: 'conversum fuit mihi in dulcedinem animi et corporis' — confirm 'dulcedo' and its pronunciation (ecclesiastical Latin).
Mark 1:40–42 paraphrased: Jesus touches the leper before healing him.
